cues.text: A Professional Thief
In 1412, a man named Jan van Langerstede made his living stealing sacred objects from churches to resell across Europe.
He broke into the church at Poederle, near Herentals in what is now Belgium, and made off with a chalice and ciborium containing five consecrated Hosts.
A Restrained Getaway
As he made his way back to his lodgings at Herentals, Jan felt himself inexplicably restrained, unable to continue his journey with the stolen goods in hand.
He hid the Hosts in a field, inside a large rabbit burrow, before quietly continuing on to Herentals alone.
A Confession on the Scaffold

Jan was soon arrested when police, searching his belongings after a wave of local thefts, found the stolen chalice and ciborium among his possessions; he confessed to the theft but initially withheld what he had done with the Hosts themselves.
Sentenced to hang, he had already climbed the scaffold when, urged by the attending priest to make a full confession before dying, he finally revealed where he had hidden them.
The presiding judge suspended the execution and ordered Jan taken back to the field to point out the exact spot.
Found Whole After Eight Days
A large crowd followed the condemned man back to the field.
There, the Hosts were found arranged in the form of a cross and surrounded by a bright light—intact and undamaged despite eight days of exposure to open weather, including rain.
They were carried back in solemn procession, some to Herentals and some to Poederle, where they remained venerated for over a century, until the sixteenth.
On January 2, 1441, the magistrate of Herentals formally declared the event authentic.
Legacy
A small chapel known as De Hegge was built at the site where the Hosts were recovered, drawing visits over the centuries from bishops and, in 1749, Pope Benedict XIV himself.
Two commemorative paintings of the miracle are kept today in the collegiate church of Sint-Waldetrudiskerk in Herentals.
They are still processed to the field each year for a commemorative Mass, a devotion that has run, largely unbroken, for more than six centuries.
It began after a professional thief's theft was undone by his own conscience on the scaffold.
